body.back: Melanocortin neurons. POMC neurons release α-MSH acting on MC3/MC4 receptors in the paraventricular nucleus to stop eating; leptin stimulates them.
Cyanide inhibits Complex IV: respiration inhibited, O2 use and ATP fall. DNP uncouples: O2 use and heat rise, ATP falls.

Minerals, most vitamins, 9 amino acids, linoleic (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic (omega-3) acids, water.
Histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.back: Lipoprotein lipase. Removes lipids from chylomicrons; triglycerides are stored in adipocytes or used by cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.back: VLDL. Very low-density lipoproteins produced by the liver.

title: Body fat and fat's share of resting energy?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Body fat and fat's share of resting energy?
body.back: Men 15%, women 25%; fat supplies 80-90% of resting needs.

title: Why is fat the better energy store?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Why is fat the better energy store?
body.back: Hydrophobic and compact; 9 kcal/g vs 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate.
Using fat spares glucose for neurons and spares protein from being burnt.
A, D, E, K; less than 20 g fat/day risks deficiency.
Hydrophilic shell of proteins, phospholipids, cholesterol; hydrophobic core of TG and cholesterol.

subject: subj:physio

body.back: Chylomicron 75-1 200 nm, TG 90%; VLDL 30-80 nm, TG 55%; LDL 18-25 nm, cholesterol 53%; HDL 5-12 nm, protein 50%.
LDL delivers cholesterol to cells; HDL removes excess cholesterol to the liver.
Regular aerobic exercise; avoid smoking, saturated fats, coffee, stress.
Fatty acids: fuel, membrane flexibility, eicosanoids. Cholesterol: no energy, membrane rigidity, steroids, vitamin D.

subject: subj:physio

body.back: Oxygen. Final electron acceptor; each O atom takes 2 electrons and 2 protons to form metabolic water.
Structural components, nucleic acid backbone, cell signalling, major energy source.
1, 2, 3-10, more than 10 monomers.

body.back: Satiety. Wild type: leptin → satiety → food intake regulation.
Weight more than 20% above the recommended norm for age, sex and height.
kg/m²; 20-25 optimal; over 25 overweight; above 30 obese.

title: Three failure points of leptin signalling?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Three failure points of leptin signalling?
body.back: No leptin (ob mutation), abnormal BBB transporter, abnormal receptor (Ob-R).
Ob/ob: no leptin → no satiety → always hungry. Wild type: leptin → satiety → intake regulated.
Leptin inhibits insulin secretion; insulin stimulates leptin secretion.
Brain receptors, indexes fat stores like leptin, but weaker appetite effect.
Total: desirable below 5.0, high above 6.2. LDL desirable below 2.6. Heart disease/diabetes: total ≤ 4.5, LDL ≤ 2.5 mmol/L.
HDL too low below 1.0 (M) / 1.2 (F). Triglycerides normal below 1.7 mmol/L.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Presynaptic action potential. Arrives at the axon terminal purely by electrical conduction along the axon.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Receptor activation. Transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Calcium entry. Depolarization of the terminal opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ entry is the trigger for release.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Axon hillock. Keeps score of all EPSPs and IPSPs; an action potential fires only if the sum reaches threshold (-50 to -55 mV).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Postsynaptic ion channels. Binding opens channels: Na⁺ in gives excitation, Cl⁻ in gives inhibition.

subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ending the signal. Active reuptake into the terminal or glia, enzymatic breakdown (acetylcholinesterase) and diffusion out of the cleft.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Postsynaptic potential. A graded potential of about ±10 mV: EPSP (depolarizing) or IPSP (hyperpolarizing).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neurotransmitter release. Ca²⁺ causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their transmitter by exocytosis.
AP reaches terminal → Ca²⁺ entry → transmitter exocytosis → receptor binding → ion channels open → graded potential (PSP).
EPSP: positive ions in (Na⁺), depolarizes. IPSP: negative ions in (Cl⁻), hyperpolarizes.
Serotonin → cAMP → K⁺ channels blocked → longer presynaptic AP → more Ca²⁺ → more release.
1st: receptor to dorsal horn/medulla. 2nd: crosses, to thalamus. 3rd: thalamus to cortex.
Rest -70 mV; threshold -50 to -55 mV; each PSP about ±10 mV.
Temporal: one neuron, repeated rapid firing. Spatial: many neurons, same time, different sites.
Glutamate; GABA (and glycine).
ACh; biogenic amines (catecholamines, serotonin); amino acids (glutamate, glycine, GABA); peptides (endorphins, substance P); ATP and gases (NO).
Direct = ion channel, fast (ACh, amino acids). Indirect = second messenger, slow and long-lasting (amines, peptides, gases).

title: Three ways to end the signal?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Three ways to end the signal?
body.back: Reuptake (active transport), enzymes (AChE), diffusion.
AChE: ACh → acetate + choline. Choline taken back; ChAT: choline + acetyl CoA → ACh.
Tonic: slow/no adaptation, continuous firing (proprioceptors). Phasic: fast adaptation, bursts (touch, smell, temperature).
The study of the functional properties of neurons, glia and networks. Information from peripheral receptors is analysed by the brain into perceptions, some stored in memory, and initiates behaviour.

title: Give the four functions of CSF.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the four functions of CSF.
body.back: Protection: cushions blows. Buoyancy: reduces the brain's net weight from about 1400 g to 50 g. Excretion: one-way flow into blood removes metabolites and drugs. Endocrine medium: carries hormones to remote brain sites.
Abnormal accumulation of CSF in the ventricles, raising intracranial pressure; in childhood it can enlarge the head and cause convulsions, tunnel vision and mental disability.

Sympathetic: pupils dilated, slight saliva, pancreas inhibited, gut less motile, bladder sphincter contracted, heart faster and stronger, coronaries and bronchi dilated, spleen contracted, skin vessels constricted. Parasympathetic: the opposite, with copious saliva and a slower heart.

title: Give the neurotransmitters of the autonomic system.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the neurotransmitters of the autonomic system.
body.back: ACh at all autonomic ganglia (nicotinic) and all parasympathetic terminals (muscarinic). NE at most sympathetic terminals (alpha or beta adrenergic). Adrenaline is a hormone from the adrenal medulla.

title: How were muscarinic and nicotinic receptors defined?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How were muscarinic and nicotinic receptors defined?
body.back: Smooth muscle responds to ACh and muscarine: muscarinic receptors. Skeletal muscle responds to ACh and nicotine: nicotinic receptors.

Sweat glands: postganglionic fibres release ACh (sympathetic cholinergic). Renal vessels: postganglionic fibres release dopamine. Adrenal gland: preganglionic fibres synapse directly on it via nicotinic receptors, and it releases adrenaline and noradrenaline 4:1 into the blood.

title: Why does the autonomic system need a peripheral synapse?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Why does the autonomic system need a peripheral synapse?
body.back: Autonomic CNS axons end in autonomic ganglia; only the ganglion neurons reach the organs. The CNS controls skeletal muscle directly through the neuromuscular junction, but it has no direct influence on smooth muscle and glands without at least one peripheral synapse.

31 pairs, leaving through the intervertebral foramina. Dorsal branches serve the back, ventral ones the front and sides; branches join into plexuses. Cervical C1 to C4 and brachial C5 to T1; thoracic T1 to T12; lumbar L1 to L4; sacral and coccygeal plexuses below.

title: What are the neural tracts of the cord?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What are the neural tracts of the cord?
body.back: White matter forms three columns (funiculi) on each side: posterior, anterior and lateral. Ascending tracts carry sensation up; descending tracts carry motor commands down.

title: Describe local circuit neurons of the cord.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe local circuit neurons of the cord.
body.back: Those supplying the medial ventral horn span many segments and end bilaterally, controlling posture. Those supplying the lateral ventral horn span few segments and end on the same side, for fine control of the distal limbs.

Historically by electrophysiology, from the EEG to intracellular recording. Today also with chemistry (calcium imaging), physics (fMRI) and molecular biology (site-directed mutations), since electrical events cannot be separated from their biochemistry.

Dermatome: skin whose cutaneous fibres all track to one spinal level, though they may travel in different nerves. Myotome: the muscles supplied by one set of spinal nerves. Both localise lesions; cord section causes paralysis and sensory loss below the lesion.

Merkel: slowly adapting, about 25%, epidermal, form and texture. Meissner: rapidly adapting, about 40%, motion and grip. Pacinian: rapidly adapting, 10 to 15%, deep, vibration. Ruffini: slowly adapting, deep, skin stretch.

Ia and II: proprioception, 13 to 20 µm, 80 to 120 m/s. A-beta: touch, 6 to 12 µm, 35 to 75 m/s. A-delta: pain and temperature, 1 to 5 µm, 5 to 30 m/s. C: pain, temperature and itch, unmyelinated, 0.2 to 1.5 µm, 0.5 to 2 m/s.

title: Describe the conduction pathways of the cord.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the conduction pathways of the cord.
body.back: Direct motor: lateral and anterior corticospinal and corticobulbar, for voluntary movement. Indirect motor: rubrospinal, tectospinal, vestibulospinal, lateral and medial reticulospinal, for automatic movement and tone. Spinothalamic: pain, temperature, itch, crude touch. Posterior column: discriminative touch, vibration, conscious proprioception.

Nociceptors are specialised neurons, with a threshold near 45°C. First sharp pain in A-delta fibres, second burning pain in C fibres. Primary afferents run in Lissauer's tract; C fibres end in laminae 1 and 2, A-delta in 1 and 5; second-order neurons cross and ascend in the anterolateral column.

title: Describe the two aspects of pain.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the two aspects of pain.
body.back: Sensory-discriminative: location, intensity and quality, via the somatosensory cortex. Affective-motivational: unpleasantness, fear and autonomic activation, via the cingulate and insular cortex, amygdala and hypothalamus.

title: Peripheral versus central sensitisation, and the gate theory.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Peripheral versus central sensitisation, and the gate theory.
body.back: Peripheral: nociceptors sensitised by the inflammatory soup (bradykinin, prostaglandins, histamine, 5-HT, substance P). Central: activity-dependent rise in dorsal horn excitability. Gate theory: mechanoreceptor (A-beta) input inhibits nociceptive transmission via inhibitory interneurons; descending enkephalin neurons also block it.

Free nerve endings are ancient, unspecialised, in skin, mucosa and viscera, with a high threshold for pain and temperature. Specialised receptors are newer, in the dermis, joints, muscles and tendons, wrapped in modified Schwann cells, with a low threshold for touch, pressure, vibration and stretch.

title: How is the nervous system organised?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How is the nervous system organised?
body.back: CNS: brain and spinal cord, the control centre. PNS: cranial and spinal nerves, ganglia and sensory organs, carrying signals in and out. The PNS has somatic (voluntary, skeletal muscle), autonomic (involuntary, smooth and cardiac muscle and glands) and enteric (gut) parts; the autonomic has sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest) divisions.

title: What do the brain and spinal cord do?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What do the brain and spinal cord do?
body.back: Brain: receives and processes sensation, initiates responses, stores memories, generates thought and emotion. Spinal cord: conducts signals to and from the brain and controls reflexes.

title: Name the landmarks dividing the four lobes.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the landmarks dividing the four lobes.
body.back: Central sulcus: frontal from parietal. Lateral (Sylvian) fissure: temporal below frontal and parietal. Parieto-occipital sulcus: parietal from occipital. Gyri are crests, sulci the grooves between them.

Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex (planning, initiating, directing) and brainstem centres (basic movement, posture) act on local circuit neurons and lower motor neuron pools in the cord and brainstem. The basal ganglia gate the initiation of movement; the cerebellum coordinates ongoing movement.

title: Describe the extrapyramidal tracts in this lecture.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the extrapyramidal tracts in this lecture.
body.back: Rubrospinal: activates flexors, inhibits extensors. Pontine reticulospinal: activates both. Medullary reticulospinal: inhibits both. Lateral vestibulospinal (Deiters' nucleus): activates extensors, inhibits flexors. Tectospinal: controls neck muscles.

Choroid plexus, lateral ventricles, foramen of Monro, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, foramen of Magendie, subarachnoid space, arachnoid granulations, superior sagittal sinus and venous circulation. There is also lymphatic drainage along the cranial nerves.

Three layers around the brain and cord: dura (outermost), arachnoid (with trabeculae) and pia (applied to the brain surface). Because the pia follows every fold and the arachnoid does not, the subarachnoid space enlarges into cisterns of CSF.

title: Which part of the grey matter is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which part of the grey matter is at the arrow?
body.back: The dorsal horn, where sensory input, including pain fibres in Rexed laminae 1, 2 and 5, arrives.

title: Which part is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which part is at the arrow?
body.back: The ventral horn, with the lower motor neuron pools: medial for posture, lateral for distal limbs.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The dorsal root and its ganglion: sensory input into the cord.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The ventral root, carrying motor output from the cord.
The white matter, organised in three funiculi on each side carrying the ascending and descending tracts.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fascicle. A bundle of muscle fibres wrapped in perimysium.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Muscle fibre. One multinucleate cell formed by fusion of 100 or more myoblasts; its number is fixed at birth.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Whole muscle. Attached to bone by tendons; wrapped in epimysium.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Myofibril. Lengthwise subdivision of the fibre, made of myofilaments in repeating sarcomeres.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sarcomere. The functional unit, from one Z disc to the next; it shortens during contraction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thick filament. About 250 myosin II molecules; about 16 nm wide.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thin filament. Actin polymer with the regulatory proteins tropomyosin and troponin; about 8 nm wide.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Structural proteins. Titin is elastic and anchors myosin to the Z disc; nebulin is non-elastic along actin; CapZ caps actin at the Z disc.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Triad. One T-tubule between two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which store and release Ca²⁺.

title: Skeletal vs smooth vs cardiac: nuclei and striations?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Skeletal vs smooth vs cardiac: nuclei and striations?
body.back: Skeletal: many peripheral nuclei, striated. Smooth: one central nucleus, not striated. Cardiac: one central nucleus, striated, intercalated discs.

title: Ca²⁺ source and binding protein by muscle type?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Ca²⁺ source and binding protein by muscle type?
body.back: Skeletal: SR, troponin. Smooth: SR + ECF, calmodulin. Cardiac: SR + ECF, troponin.
Isotonic: shortens, load moves. Isometric: tension without shortening.
Contractility, conductivity, excitability, extensibility, elasticity.
One T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the SR.
Contractile (actin, myosin), regulatory (tropomyosin, troponin), structural (titin, nebulin, CapZ).
Myosin (muscle), kinesin (organelles on microtubules), dynein (cilia, flagella).
Hexamer: 2 heavy + 4 light chains. Head (S1) has the ATP and actin sites; neck is the lever arm (5-10 nm stroke).
Z = zwischen (between), I = isotropic, A = anisotropic, H = helles (clear), M = mittel (middle).
Sarcomere, I band, H zone. A band and filament lengths stay the same.
DHP: voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel in the T-tubule. Ryanodine: Ca²⁺ release channel of the SR, gated by DHP.
Synaptic vesicles of ACh, about 1000 molecules in each.

title: Which channel is at the arrow, and what does it trigger?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which channel is at the arrow, and what does it trigger?
body.back: The voltage-gated Ca2+ channel of the nerve terminal; Ca2+ entry triggers ACh release.

title: Which space is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which space is at the arrow?
body.back: The synaptic cleft, about 50 nm wide, crossed by ACh in about 0.5 ms.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The motor end plate, with nicotinic ACh receptors clustered in the junctional folds.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The T-tubule, carrying the action potential inward; its DHP receptors sense the depolarization.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The sarcoplasmic reticulum, which stores Ca2+ and releases it through ryanodine receptors.

One motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates, about 50 to 500 fibres, which contract together. One neuron can supply many fibres, but each fibre has only one neuron. The gastrocnemius has about 300 motor units.

Skeletal: no intrinsic activity, a highly reliable end plate potential, fast through T-tubules and DHP-ryanodine coupling. Smooth: an intrinsic slow wave, slow because it lacks T-tubules and uses calmodulin and MLCK; relaxed by nitric oxide via cGMP. Cardiac: an intrinsic pacemaker potential, intermediate speed through Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release.
MLCK is activated, myosin is phosphorylated and its ATPase activity rises. This covalent change can be sustained for long-term contraction.

title: Give the three energy sources for muscle.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the three energy sources for muscle.
body.back: The sarcoplasm holds ATP for only about 8 twitches. It is regenerated by the creatine kinase (phosphocreatine) shunt, which keeps ADP/ATP low, and by glycolysis and oxidative metabolism.
A fibre obeys the all or none principle. Its tension depends on the number of pivoting cross-bridges, its resting length at stimulation and the stimulation frequency.

Cross-bridge number depends on the overlap of thick and thin filaments. Optimal overlap gives the greatest tension; too much or too little reduces it. Normal resting sarcomere length is 75 to 130 percent of optimal.
Mainly by recruiting motor units, the most important means, and by increasing stimulation frequency. The fewer fibres per motor unit, the finer the movement.

All fibres in a motor unit are the same type. Slow units: myosin with a long cycle time, many mitochondria, economical sustained force. Fast units: rapid cycling myosin for high power; type 2A fast and sustained, type 2X faster but non-oxidative and quickly fatigued.

title: How does muscle adapt to use and disuse?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How does muscle adapt to use and disuse?
body.back: Muscle is plastic. Endurance training brings little hypertrophy but more mitochondria and oxidative enzymes. Strength training brings hypertrophy. Disuse, from bed rest, casting, denervation or space flight, causes fibre atrophy without fibre loss, most marked in type II fibres and reversible in the young.
Isotonic: the muscle shortens against a constant load. Isometric: the muscle develops tension without changing length.

title: Describe the muscle twitch and summation.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the muscle twitch and summation.
body.back: A twitch has lag, contraction and relaxation phases. Each fibre obeys the all or none law, but the whole muscle is graded by motor unit summation. As frequency rises, contractions summate: incomplete tetanus when the fibre partly relaxes, fused tetanus when it cannot.

A chemical synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal fibre. The presynaptic terminal holds vesicles of about 1000 ACh molecules each. The cleft is about 50 nm, crossed in about 0.5 ms. The postsynaptic motor end plate carries clusters of nicotinic receptors in junctional folds.
A graded response in a muscle rested for a long time: each contraction is stronger than the last until they level off after a few stimuli.

The inability to maintain the desired power output, when ATP use exceeds ATP synthesis. Causes: depletion of reserves, low pH from lactate, low glycogen, and damage to the sarcolemma and SR. Types: psychological, muscular (ATP depletion) and synaptic (lack of ACh).

title: Why do fats burn in the flame of carbohydrates?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Why do fats burn in the flame of carbohydrates?
body.back: Even when fatty acids are being oxidised, glucose metabolism is needed to supply pyruvate, which becomes oxaloacetate to keep the TCA cycle turning. So when muscle glycogen runs out, endurance athletes hit the wall; carbohydrate loading beforehand raises stamina.

Fatigue: only about 30 percent of ATP is depleted; there is enough to pump Ca2+ but ADP/ATP is too high for cross-bridges. Rigor mortis: complete ATP depletion, so no Ca2+ transport and no cross-bridge detachment; it begins about 3 hours after death and lasts up to 72 hours.

title: Compare type I, IIa and IIb fibres.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Compare type I, IIa and IIb fibres.
body.back: Type I: slow oxidative, low glycogen, high mitochondria (50 percent), high myoglobin (red), high capillaries, used for hours, highly fatigue resistant, small. Type IIa: fast oxidative-glycolytic, intermediate, under 30 minutes. Type IIb: fast glycolytic, high glycogen, low mitochondria (20 percent), white, under 5 minutes, large.

Strength training uses 75 to 90 percent of maximal force, gives few biochemical changes but hypertrophy through more sarcomeric protein. Endurance training uses 15 to 20 percent of maximal force and gives more and larger mitochondria, glycogen, myoglobin, capillaries and enzymes such as GLUT4, delaying fatigue and improving blood glucose in diabetes.

Both are autosomal recessive glycogen storage myopathies with cramps, fatigue, myalgia and myoglobinuria on strenuous exercise. McArdle (type V): no muscle glycogen phosphorylase, no lactate rise, a characteristic second wind; treated with sucrose before exercise and gentle aerobic exercise. Tarui (type VII): no muscle PFK; avoid strenuous exercise.

Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune suppression of the postsynaptic nicotinic receptors, classically treated with AChE inhibitors. Lambert-Eaton: autoimmune attack on the presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, blocking ACh release.
A degenerative motor neuron disease with muscle atrophy; about 10 percent of cases are genetic, the rest of unknown, possibly environmental, cause; frequency about 5 per 100,000.

X-linked recessive (Xp21), lacking dystrophin, so fibres lose integrity and are replaced by fat and fibrous tissue. A young boy falls, waddles, pushes up with his arms to stand, with proximal weakness and calf hypertrophy. CK is markedly raised; genetic testing and biopsy confirm. Walking is usually lost by 10, life expectancy is about 25, with cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure. Becker is milder, with partly functional dystrophin.

title: List the events at the NMJ.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: List the events at the NMJ.
body.back: 1. A neuronal action potential. 2. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open. 3. ACh is released. 4. ACh diffuses and binds its receptor. 5. The cation pore opens and Na+ enters. 6. An end plate potential develops. 7. AChE splits ACh into choline and acetate; choline returns by Na+-coupled transport.
Bound to the end plate facing the cleft, it rapidly breaks ACh into inactive acetate and choline, ending the EPP. Its activity is not regulated, so longer stimulation requires more ACh.

A ligand-gated cation channel permeable to Ca2+, Na+ and K+, with the largest driving force for Na+ and Ca2+, giving net depolarization. Two ACh molecules bind the two α subunits to open it, producing the end plate potential.

title: From mEPP to EPP to action potential.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: From mEPP to EPP to action potential.
body.back: One vesicle gives a miniature EPP of about 0.5 mV. About 100 vesicles sum to an EPP of about 50 mV. The EPP spreads passively to nearby membrane, which reaches threshold and fires an action potential through voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels.

title: Give the steps of excitation-contraction coupling.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the steps of excitation-contraction coupling.
body.back: 1. Action potentials propagate along the T-tubules. 2. L-type Ca2+ channels, the DHP receptors, open. 3. They trigger the ryanodine receptors of the SR to release Ca2+. 4. Ca2+ binds troponin, unmasking the myosin sites on actin. 5. SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the SR.

title: Give the calcium numbers in muscle.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the calcium numbers in muscle.
body.back: Resting cytosol holds about 0.1 µmol/L of Ca2+; the SR can hold 10,000 times more. When the SR channels open, cytosolic Ca2+ rises 10-fold or more.

title: What structures are involved in EC coupling?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What structures are involved in EC coupling?
body.back: The sarcolemma, the transverse (T) tubules, the terminal cisternae, the sarcoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+ and troponin.

title: Which receptor is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which receptor is at the arrow?
body.back: The muscle spindle, the stretch receptor that starts the myotatic reflex.

title: Which fibre is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which fibre is at the arrow?
body.back: The Ia afferent, carrying the stretch signal from the spindle to the spinal cord.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.back: The dorsal root ganglion, holding the cell body of the T-shaped sensory neuron.

title: Which neuron is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which neuron is at the arrow?
body.back: The alpha motor neuron, from the ventral horn to the quadriceps, making it contract.

title: Which cell is at the arrow, and what does it do?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which cell is at the arrow, and what does it do?
body.back: The inhibitory interneuron, which relaxes the antagonist hamstrings: reciprocal inhibition.

title: What happens to the muscle at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What happens to the muscle at the arrow?
body.back: The hamstrings, the antagonist, relax through reciprocal inhibition as the quadriceps contracts.

title: Name the three types of motor activity.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the three types of motor activity.
body.back: Reflex: elementary, innate, involuntary, a stereotyped response to a specific stimulus. Automatic activity: innate but under the will, adaptable, mostly rhythmic, such as breathing, walking and chewing. Deliberate motricity: based on habits and programmes, always modulated by the cortex.
0 no response; 1+ visible but diminished; 2+ normal; 3+ stronger than average; 4+ hyperactive.

A stimulus at the popliteal fossa first travels down motor fibres to the soleus, recorded as the M wave. The same stimulus sends Ia afferents to the motor neuron in the cord, whose output reaches the soleus later as the H-reflex. It is recorded by electroneuromyography.

title: What does an electromyogram show about the reflex?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What does an electromyogram show about the reflex?
body.back: An EMG during an Achilles reflex, compared with a voluntary contraction of the triceps surae, shows that the spinal cord is the nerve centre of the myotatic reflex.

title: What is proprioception, and which receptors serve it?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is proprioception, and which receptors serve it?
body.back: The perception of one's body in movement and position. Receptors: the neuromuscular spindle (length), the Golgi tendon organ (tension), joint kinesthetic receptors and the vestibular apparatus.

An elongated fusiform receptor in parallel with the muscle, the main mechanoreceptor of proprioception. Contraction unloads it and stretch stimulates it. It holds four to eight intrafusal fibres around the sensory element, with motor and sensory innervation. It senses length and amplitude of stretch (static) and speed of stretch (dynamic).
Multinucleated, with contractile poles and a non-contractile central part containing nuclei. Three types: nuclear chain fibres, static nuclear bag fibres and dynamic nuclear bag fibres.
Ia: 17 µm, 70 to 110 m/s, innervating both bag and chain fibres at the equator, signalling length and speed. II: 8 µm, 30 to 70 m/s, mainly chain fibres, signalling length only.
Primary (Ia) endings transmit limb dynamics: the velocity and direction of movement. Secondary (II) endings transmit the static position of the limbs.

Two neuronal populations: T-shaped afferent neurons from the spindles, connected in the cord to motor neurons of the same muscle. Two synapses: neuron to neuron in the cord, and the neuromuscular junction.

Reflex contraction of the agonist is accompanied by inhibition of the antagonist through an inhibitory interneuron. In a knee jerk the quadriceps (extensor) contracts and the hamstrings (flexors) relax.

An involuntary, relatively stereotyped response to a specific sensory stimulus. The location of the stimulus fixes which muscle contracts; its strength sets the amplitude, so reflexes are graded. The reflex arc is the neural mechanism behind it.

title: What do gamma motor neurons do?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What do gamma motor neurons do?
body.back: Small ventral horn neurons whose fibres contract the ends of intrafusal fibres. This keeps the spindle sensitive by matching its length to the muscle's during contraction.
When alpha motor neurons contract the extrafusal fibres, gamma motor neurons contract the spindle ends at the same time, so the spindle stays taut and keeps signalling.

title: How does the brain use the spindle?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How does the brain use the spindle?
body.back: Collaterals of the sensory axon tell the brain about muscle stretch, helping it coordinate movement and posture, and letting it know a reflex happened. Through gamma motor neurons the brain sets spindle sensitivity and overall tone, raising it for fast, difficult movements such as a gymnast on a beam.

title: Describe the tendon, flexor and crossed extensor reflexes.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the tendon, flexor and crossed extensor reflexes.
body.back: Tendon reflex: polysynaptic; the tendon organ detects excess tension, an inhibitory interneuron relaxes the muscle and an excitatory one contracts the antagonist. Flexor (withdrawal) reflex: stepping on a tack activates interneurons in several segments, flexors contract and the leg withdraws. Crossed extensor reflex: the opposite leg extends to take the weight.

Leg extension by quadriceps contraction in response to tapping the patellar ligament. Blocked by damage to its nerves or to L2 to L4; often absent in chronic diabetes or neurosyphilis; exaggerated with descending motor tract disease.

Plantar flexion by gastrocnemius and soleus after tapping the calcaneal tendon. Absence indicates damage to the posterior leg nerves or lumbosacral neurons, and can occur in diabetes, neurosyphilis, alcoholism and subarachnoid haemorrhage. Exaggeration indicates cervical cord compression or a lesion of the motor tracts at S1 or S2.

Stroking the lateral sole extends the great toe, with or without fanning. Normal under 1.5 years because the corticospinal tract is not yet myelinated; after that it indicates a corticospinal lesion. The normal adult response is plantar flexion of all the toes.

title: Name the paralyses from cord lesions at different levels.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the paralyses from cord lesions at different levels.
body.back: Monoplegia, diplegia, paraplegia, hemiplegia and tetraplegia, with sensory loss in the dermatomes below the lesion.

Autonomic: started in the viscera, carried by autonomic nerves to soft tissue organs, running gut and reproductive contractions, pupil dilation, defecation and vomiting. Somatic: started at somatic sensory endings, acting on skeletal muscle, protecting from injury.
A monosynaptic reflex triggered by sudden passive stretch of the muscle belly, making the agonist contract while the antagonist relaxes.

It maintains upright posture. The anti-gravity extensors of the neck, trunk and legs are stretched as these parts flex and contract reflexly, creating tone. The waiter example: water added to a tray stretches the biceps, activating spindle Ia afferents, and the reflex keeps the tray steady.

A dynamic change in muscle length, such as a tendon tap, triggers a brief phasic contraction through Ia afferents. It prevents extrafusal fibres being stretched beyond their physiological limits, as in the Achilles stretch.

title: Give the roles of the myotatic reflex.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the roles of the myotatic reflex.
body.back: Maintaining tone, maintaining posture by continuously adjusting contractions, adjusting muscle function during exercise, and preventing injury by opposing overstretching.

Hyporeflexia, absent or diminished reflexes, usually indicates disease of the two-neuron arc itself. Hyperreflexia, hyperactive or clonic reflexes, indicates interruption of the corticospinal and descending pathways by a lesion above the reflex level. Reflex changes often precede other signs of disease.

title: Name the tested tendon reflexes and their responses.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the tested tendon reflexes and their responses.
body.back: Patellar: quadriceps, leg extension. Achilles: soleus, foot extension. Bicipital: biceps, forearm flexion. Tricipital: triceps, forearm extension.

title: Which part of the graph is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which part of the graph is at the arrow?
body.back: The resting potential, about -70 mV, with leak K+ channels open and voltage-gated channels closed.

title: Which point is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which point is at the arrow?
body.back: Threshold, about -50 to -55 mV, where voltage-gated Na+ channels open and the action potential begins.

title: Which phase is at the arrow, and what causes it?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which phase is at the arrow, and what causes it?
body.back: The rising phase, depolarization, caused by Na+ rushing in through voltage-gated Na+ channels.

title: Which point is at the arrow?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which point is at the arrow?
body.back: The peak of the action potential, when Na+ channels inactivate and K+ channels are opening.

title: Which phase is at the arrow, and what causes it?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which phase is at the arrow, and what causes it?
body.back: The falling phase, repolarization, caused by K+ flowing out through voltage-gated K+ channels.

title: Which phase is at the arrow, and why does it happen?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which phase is at the arrow, and why does it happen?
body.back: The afterhyperpolarization: the slow K+ channels close late, so the membrane dips below rest before recovering.

title: Name the two cell categories of the nervous system and the glial types.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the two cell categories of the nervous system and the glial types.
body.back: Neurons, the signalling cells, and neuroglia, which support development, growth, survival and structure: ependymal cells, astrocytes, Schwann cells, oligodendrocytes and microglia.

Tapering, branching extensions of the soma, with dendritic spines in the cerebral and cerebellar cortex. There may be none, one or many. They conduct toward the cell body, generate local rather than action potentials, contain Nissl granules and neurofibrils, and with the soma form the input zone.

Only one per neuron, arising from the axon hillock and carrying impulses away from the soma. It cannot make its own protein. It branches only at its end, the synaptic knob or terminal button. It may be myelinated or not, contains transmitter vesicles, and converts the electrical signal into a chemical one.

The axoplasm, the central core of cytoplasm, together with the axolemma, its membrane, continuous with the cell membrane of the soma. It contains mitochondria, neurofibrils and vesicles, and is covered by neurilemma in unmyelinated fibres or by myelin in myelinated ones.

title: Name the three types of synapse.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the three types of synapse.
body.back: Neuron to neuron (synapse), neuron to skeletal muscle (neuromuscular junction) and neuron to gland (neuroglandular synapse).
Electrically, by ions moving across membranes, locally or over long distances; and chemically, by releasing neurotransmitters onto receptors at synapses.

title: Name the ion channel types in neurons.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the ion channel types in neurons.
body.back: Mechanically gated (physical force), voltage-gated (membrane potential), ligand-gated (a chemical binds) and leak channels (always open). Phosphorylation-gated channels stay open while a phosphate is attached.

title: Give the key properties of ion channels.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the key properties of ion channels.
body.back: Transmembrane protein pores. Flux is always passive, up to a million ions per second. Most are gated. Opening is a conformational change; once open, no further change is needed. They are selective by charge (a positive charge in the pore passes anions) and by size (Na+ versus K+).

The electrical charge inside the cell compared with outside. Positive when the inside is more positive; negative when the inside is less positive. Measured in millivolts; charges accumulate right at the membrane and cannot cross the lipid bilayer without channels.

Resting potential: maintained across excitable membranes. Hyperpolarization: more negative than rest. Depolarization: less negative or positive. Threshold: the depolarization that triggers an action potential. Action potential: a rapid, large regenerative depolarization. Repolarization: return to rest.

title: Why is the resting potential -70 mV?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Why is the resting potential -70 mV?
body.back: Negative proteins inside, a moderate K+ concentration inside and a high Na+ concentration outside. At rest K+ leak channels are open, so K+ permeability is high, while few Na+ channels are open, so Na+ permeability is low.

title: Give the four functional zones of a neuron.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the four functional zones of a neuron.
body.back: 1. Input zone: dendrites and cell body receive signals. 2. Trigger zone: the axon hillock initiates action potentials. 3. Conducting zone: the axon, 1 mm to over 1 m long, conducts without decrement. 4. Output zone: axon terminals release neurotransmitter.

title: What are the forces on K+ and Na+?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What are the forces on K+ and Na+?
body.back: K+: the concentration gradient pushes it out, the negative interior holds it in; equilibrium about -90 mV. Na+: both the concentration gradient and the negative interior pull it in; equilibrium about +60 mV. Nothing moves without channels.

Graded: small, local, variable in size and proportional to the stimulus, fading with distance, excitatory (positive ions in) or inhibitory (negative ions in or positive ions out). Action potential: large, fast, all or none, the same every time, spreading without decrement one way down the axon.

title: Give the six phases of the action potential.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the six phases of the action potential.
body.back: 1. Rest at -70 mV. 2. Threshold reached. 3. Rising phase: depolarization. 4. Falling phase: repolarization. 5. Dip: afterhyperpolarization. 6. Return to rest.

title: Describe the voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels.
body.back: Na+: closed at -70 mV, opening rapidly at -50 to -55 mV, closed by a separate inactivation gate. K+: closed at -70 mV, opening slowly at -50 to -55 mV and closing slowly, which causes the dip below rest.

title: How does an action potential propagate?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How does an action potential propagate?
body.back: It starts at the axon hillock. Na+ rushing in brings neighbouring membrane to threshold, opening more Na+ channels in a domino effect. It moves only toward the axon terminal, because the Na+ channels behind it are temporarily inactivated.

Myelination, which insulates the axon, and axon diameter, since a larger diameter means lower resistance. Large axons reach 120 m/s, for skeletal muscle; small ones only 0.7 m/s, for the gut. Fast axons are both large and myelinated.

Myelin, from oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS, is up to 300 layers thick, with no channels beneath it and gaps called nodes of Ranvier. Voltage-gated channels cluster at the nodes, so the signal jumps from node to node, faster and needing fewer Na+/K+ pumps.

title: Give some numbers about the nervous system.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give some numbers about the nervous system.
body.back: The human CNS contains over 100 billion neurons and 50 to 100 times as many glial cells; about 40 percent of human genes take part in its formation. With the endocrine system it forms the major control system of the body.

title: How do neurons differ from other cells?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How do neurons differ from other cells?
body.back: They have processes (dendrites and an axon), Nissl granules and neurofibrillae, no centrosome so they cannot divide, and they contain and secrete neurotransmitters.

title: Describe the neuronal domains and their channels.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the neuronal domains and their channels.
body.back: Dendrites receive signals through ligand-gated and GPCR-gated channels. The cell body carries out biosynthesis and integration. The axon hillock generates action potentials. The axon conducts impulses with voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels. The nerve terminals secrete neurotransmitter with voltage-gated Na+, Ca2+ and K+ channels.

By number of poles; by function (motor or efferent, with a long axon and short dendrites, carrying impulses from the CNS; sensory or afferent, with a short axon and long dendrites, carrying impulses to the CNS); and by axon length (Golgi type I, long axons to remote organs; Golgi type II, short axons in the cortex and cord).

Also called soma or perikaryon, stellate, round or pyramidal, maintaining the integrity of the axon. It contains the nucleus, Nissl bodies, neurofibrillae, mitochondria and the Golgi apparatus. Somata lie in the grey matter and the nuclei and ganglia; no process survives without its soma.

title: Describe the nucleus and Nissl granules.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the nucleus and Nissl granules.
body.back: One central nucleus with prominent nucleoli rich in RNA; no centrosome, so no division. Nissl granules, named after Franz Nissl and called tigroid substance, are small basophilic clusters in the cell body and dendrites, absent from the axon and axon hillock.

title: Describe neurofibrillae, mitochondria and the Golgi apparatus.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe neurofibrillae, mitochondria and the Golgi apparatus.
body.back: Neurofibrillae: threads of microtubules and microfilaments throughout the cell. Mitochondria: in the soma and axon, making ATP. Golgi apparatus: processes and packages proteins into granules.

Pain (IASP): an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage. Nociception: the unconscious activity induced by a noxious stimulus applied to sense receptors. Pain is what the patient says it is.

Mechanical: strong pressure. Thermal: skin above 42°C or severe cold. Chemical: bradykinin, histamine, acidity. Polymodal: combinations. Activation depends on location: the skin responds to cutting, the viscera do not. Cool receptors are on A-delta and C fibres, warmth receptors on C fibres; itch and tickle are related to pain.

title: Why do pain receptors not adapt?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Why do pain receptors not adapt?
body.back: They adapt very little; for slow pain, excitation can even grow as the stimulus continues (hyperalgesia). This keeps the person aware of damage as long as it lasts. Pain intensity also tracks local K+ and proteolytic enzymes.

title: Why do ischaemia and spasm hurt?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Why do ischaemia and spasm hurt?
body.back: Ischaemia: pain within minutes, faster with high metabolism: 15 to 20 s in an exercised ischaemic forearm, 3 to 4 min at rest; lactic acid, bradykinin and proteolytic enzymes are blamed. Spasm: stimulates mechanosensitive endings, compresses vessels and raises metabolism, worsening ischaemia.

title: Name the chemical mediators of peripheral sensitisation.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the chemical mediators of peripheral sensitisation.
body.back: Injured cells release K+, substance P, bradykinin and prostaglandin E2. Nociceptor terminals release substance P and CGRP, triggering histamine release and vasodilation. Macrophages and epithelial cells release growth factors, IL-1β, bradykinin, ATP and H+.

title: Compare the fast and slow pain fibres.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Compare the fast and slow pain fibres.
body.back: Fast: A-delta, 6 to 30 m/s, mechanical and thermal stimuli, warns the person to withdraw. Slow: unmyelinated C, 0.5 to 2 m/s, mostly chemical stimuli, grows over time into intolerable suffering.

title: Describe the spinal connections of pain fibres.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the spinal connections of pain fibres.
body.back: Branches run 1 to 2 segments up and down in Lissauer's tract. C fibres synapse in laminae 1 and 2, A-delta in 1 and 5. Second-order axons cross the midline and ascend in the ventrolateral tract.

For fast pain. A-delta fibres end in lamina I and excite second-order neurons, whose axons cross in the anterior commissure and ascend in the anterolateral columns. A few end in the reticular brainstem; most reach the ventrobasal thalamus, then the somatosensory cortex. Transmitter: glutamate.

Older, for slow pain. C fibres end mainly in laminae II and III, the substantia gelatinosa. Only a tenth to a quarter of fibres reach the thalamus; most end in the reticular nuclei, the tectum or the periaqueductal grey. So slow pain is localised only to a large body part.

title: Why is pinprick pain felt twice?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Why is pinprick pain felt twice?
body.back: C fibres release glutamate, fast and brief, and substance P, which builds up over seconds to minutes. Glutamate may give the fast sensation, substance P the lagging one.

1. The periaqueductal and periventricular grey of the midbrain and upper pons. 2. The raphe magnus nucleus in the lower pons. 3. A pain-inhibitory complex in the dorsal horn. Stimulating the PAG or raphe magnus suppresses strong pain. Transmitters: enkephalin and serotonin.

Acute (fast) pain is local and short-lived. Chronic (pathological) pain includes neuropathic and inflammatory pain and is emotionally destructive. Risk factors for chronic neck and back pain: ageing, female sex, anxiety, repetitive work, obesity, depression, heavy lifting, nicotine.

It causes presynaptic and postsynaptic inhibition of C and A-delta fibres in the dorsal horn: less Ca2+ entry and transmitter release from the first-order neuron, K+ channel opening that hyperpolarises the second-order neuron, and a smaller EPSP.

A-beta tactile fibres activate inhibitory interneurons that block C-fibre transmission to the second-order neuron. It explains why rubbing the skin, liniments, TENS and possibly acupuncture relieve pain.

title: Describe the descending regulation of pain.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the descending regulation of pain.
body.back: The PAG contains endorphin neurons and responds to opioids. It projects to the nucleus raphe magnus and rostral ventromedial medulla. Serotoninergic and catecholaminergic pathways descend and stimulate dorsal horn enkephalin interneurons, which inhibit nociceptive transmission.

title: What is referred pain, and why does it happen?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is referred pain, and why does it happen?
body.back: Pain felt in a part of the body remote from its source, often visceral pain felt on the skin. Visceral fibres synapse on the same second-order neurons as skin fibres, so the brain attributes the pain to the skin: the convergence-projection theory. It is often the only clinical sign of visceral disease.

Caused by ischaemia, chemical damage, smooth muscle spasm, excess distension and stretching of connective tissue. Carried by C fibres, so only slow aching pain. Poorly localised, often with nausea, sweating and blood pressure changes; afferents travel with sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves; often referred.

title: Which viscera are almost insensitive to pain?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which viscera are almost insensitive to pain?
body.back: The liver parenchyma, the lung alveoli and the brain.

Nociceptive pain needs transduction of a non-electrical stimulus; most people recover, for example after surgery. Neuropathic pain comes from direct nerve stimulation or injury, such as plexopathy or amputation, and often persists. Treatments include NMDA receptor inhibitors and GABA analogues.

Discriminative: spinothalamic tract to the VPL thalamus, then S1 and S2. Affective-motivational: branches to the reticular formation, superior colliculus, PAG, hypothalamus and amygdala, and via midline thalamic nuclei to the anterior cingulate and insular cortex.
Hyperalgesia: an exaggerated response to a noxious stimulus. Allodynia: pain from a normally harmless stimulus, such as light touch of sunburned skin.

It occurs whenever tissue is being damaged and makes the person remove the stimulus. Sitting too long causes skin ischaemia; the pain makes us shift weight. After spinal cord injury the pain sense is lost, the person fails to shift, and pressure damage follows.

Fast pain: felt within 0.1 s; sharp, pricking, electric; from needles, cuts, burns and shocks in the skin; not felt in deep tissues. Slow pain: begins after 1 s or more and builds; burning, aching, throbbing, nauseous, chronic; tied to tissue destruction; in skin and almost any deep tissue.

All are free nerve endings: widespread in the superficial skin and in the periosteum, arterial walls, joint surfaces, and the falx and tentorium. Other deep tissues are sparsely supplied, but widespread damage summates into slow aching pain.

TRPV1 (VR-1): on C and A-delta fibres, activated by about 45°C and by capsaicin. TRPV2 (VRL-1): higher threshold, about 52°C, not capsaicin-sensitive, on A-delta fibres. Both belong to the transient receptor potential family, sensitive to ranges of heat and cold.

title: What three types of stimuli excite pain receptors?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What three types of stimuli excite pain receptors?
body.back: Mechanical, thermal and chemical. Chemical exciters: bradykinin, serotonin, histamine, K+, acids, ACh and proteolytic enzymes. Prostaglandins and substance P sensitise endings without exciting them. Chemicals are especially important in slow pain after injury.

title: Give the three components of pain physiology.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the three components of pain physiology.
body.back: Transduction: converting the noxious stimulus into an electrical signal. Transmission: along the nociceptive pathway. Modulation: up- or down-regulation of the signal at every relay, the sensory neuron, dorsal horn and brain, partly explaining individual differences.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Carbonic anhydrase. Enzyme that speeds the conversion between CO2 + H2O and H2CO3, in tubule cells and the lumen.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: CO2 and water. Carbon dioxide, controlled by the lungs (ventilation).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Carbonic acid. H2CO3, formed from CO2 and water and dissociating into H+ and HCO3−.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hydrogen ion and bicarbonate. H+ secretion and HCO3− reabsorption are controlled by the kidneys.
Acidosis causes hyperkalaemia: K+ shifts out of cells.
Chemical buffers (fast), lungs (CO2), kidneys (slowest; only route for non-carbonic acids).
pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3−]/(0.03 × PCO2): kidneys set HCO3−, lungs set PCO2.

title: Link between H+ secretion and HCO3−?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Link between H+ secretion and HCO3−?
body.back: Each H+ secreted goes with one HCO3− reabsorbed: urine acidification = blood alkalinisation.
Filtered HCO3− + H+ → H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O (carbonic anhydrase); CO2 enters the cell; HCO3− rebuilt and leaves with Na+.
PCT 85%, thick ascending limb 10%, distal 4.9%.

title: Lowest urine pH and the urinary buffers?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Lowest urine pH and the urinary buffers?
body.back: pH 4.5; phosphates (filtered) and ammonia (amino acid deamination).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Angiotensin II. Angiotensin-converting enzyme in the lungs and kidneys converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Aldosterone. Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Angiotensin I. Renin converts angiotensinogen, a blood protein from the liver, into angiotensin I.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fall in blood pressure. Baroreceptors in the carotid and aorta stimulate the sympathetic nervous system.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Renin. Released by the granular (juxtaglomerular) cells, triggered by sympathetic fibres.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Salt and water retention. Na+ and H2O reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct raises plasma volume and blood pressure.
Renal autoregulation, sympathetic control, hormonal control.
Myogenic mechanism (intrinsic) and tubuloglomerular feedback (extrinsic).
Myogenic: stretched afferent arteriole constricts; at low pressure it dilates, keeping flow stable.
Macula densa: NaCl chemoreceptors. Granular (JG) cells: pressure mechanoreceptors with renin.

title: Tubuloglomerular feedback when GFR is high?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Tubuloglomerular feedback when GFR is high?
body.back: More NaCl → macula densa ATP → adenosine → granular cells contract → afferent constriction → GFR ↓.
BP ↓ → sympathetic → renin → angiotensinogen to angiotensin I → ACE (lungs, kidneys) → angiotensin II.
Vasoconstriction; efferent constriction; peritubular reabsorption; aldosterone; PCT Na+ and H2O; ADH; thirst.
Afferent dilation, efferent constriction, GFR ↑, natriuresis and diuresis, renin and aldosterone ↓, vasodilation.
Angiotensinogen 453 aa → angiotensin I 10 aa → angiotensin II 8 aa.

title: How much filtrate do the kidneys form?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How much filtrate do the kidneys form?
body.back: About 2 mL per second, 120 mL per minute, about 170 to 180 L per day, 50 to 60 times the blood volume. Only 1 to 2 L of urine leaves daily, so 99 percent is reabsorbed.

title: Give GFR values for men and women.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give GFR values for men and women.
body.back: Men: about 125 mL/min or 180 L/day. Women: about 105 mL/min or 150 L/day.

title: Describe the three layers of the filtration barrier.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the three layers of the filtration barrier.
body.back: 1. Fenestrated endothelium: 70 to 90 nm pores, excludes blood cells, highly permeable. 2. Basement membrane: negatively charged proteoglycan gel, repels albumin, excludes molecules above 8 nm. 3. Filtration slits: podocyte pedicels leave 30 nm negatively charged slits.

title: What passes the filter, and what does not?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What passes the filter, and what does not?
body.back: Molecules under about 3 nm pass freely: water, electrolytes, glucose, fatty acids, amino acids, nitrogenous wastes and vitamins. Small protein-bound substances such as calcium, iron and thyroid hormone do not. Plasma is 7 percent protein; filtrate 0.03 percent.

title: What damages the filter, and what results?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What damages the filter, and what results?
body.back: Infection and trauma let albumin or blood cells through: proteinuria (albuminuria) and haematuria. Distance runners and swimmers can get temporary proteinuria or haematuria because strenuous exercise reduces renal perfusion and the glomerulus deteriorates under prolonged hypoxia.

title: Name the forces of glomerular filtration.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the forces of glomerular filtration.
body.back: Favouring: glomerular blood hydrostatic pressure. Opposing: blood colloid osmotic pressure and capsular hydrostatic pressure. Textbook values: about 60, 32 and 18 mmHg, giving a net filtration pressure of about 10 mmHg.
GFR is the filtrate formed per minute by both kidneys: GFR = NFP x Kf. Kf, the filtration coefficient, depends on the permeability and surface area of the barrier.

title: Why does hypertension harm the kidneys?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Why does hypertension harm the kidneys?
body.back: High glomerular pressure can rupture glomerular capillaries and cause scarring (nephrosclerosis) and atherosclerosis of renal vessels, ultimately leading to renal failure.

title: How do arteriolar changes alter GFR?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How do arteriolar changes alter GFR?
body.back: Textbook physiology: afferent dilation or efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure and GFR; afferent constriction or efferent dilation lowers them.

title: GFR too high versus too low.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: GFR too high versus too low.
body.back: Too high: fluid passes the tubules too fast to be reabsorbed, urine output rises, and dehydration and electrolyte depletion threaten. Too low: wastes are retained and azotemia may occur.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bladder. Stores urine until it is voided.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Kidneys. Retroperitoneal organs that filter plasma and form urine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ureters. Transport urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Urethra. Carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body.

title: Four parts of the urinary system and their roles?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Four parts of the urinary system and their roles?
body.back: Kidneys form urine; ureters transport it; bladder stores it; urethra carries it outside.
Proteins → amino acids → NH2 removed → ammonia → converted to urea by the liver.

title: Origin of uric acid and creatinine?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Origin of uric acid and creatinine?
body.back: Uric acid: nucleic acid catabolism. Creatinine: creatine phosphate catabolism.
Albuminuria, proteinuria, glucosuria, acetonuria (ketones), haematuria (RBC), pyuria (WBC).

title: What do the kidneys regulate in the blood?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What do the kidneys regulate in the blood?
body.back: Volume and pressure, osmolarity, electrolytes, acid-base balance.

title: What does EPO do and when does it rise?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What does EPO do and when does it rise?
body.back: Stimulates red cell production; rises more than 100-fold in hypoxia such as severe anaemia.
Hypoxia-inducible factor: degraded at normal O2, active in hypoxia, promotes EPO, erythropoiesis, angiogenesis.
Calcitriol (vitamin D) synthesis, which increases intestinal calcium absorption.
Gluconeogenesis from amino acids.
Filter plasma and excrete wastes; regulate volume, pressure, osmolarity, electrolytes, acid-base; EPO; calcitriol; clear hormones; detoxify free radicals; gluconeogenesis in starvation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Reabsorbs Na+ and Cl− into the interstitial fluid.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Collecting duct. Reabsorbs solutes and water from the filtrate; water permeability set by ADH.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Distal convoluted tubule. Selectively secretes and absorbs ions to keep blood pH and electrolytes balanced.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Descending limb of the loop of Henle. Aquaporins let water leave the filtrate into the interstitial fluid.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Glomerulus. Filters small solutes from the blood into Bowman's capsule.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Proximal convoluted tubule. Reabsorbs ions, water and nutrients; removes toxins and adjusts filtrate pH.

title: What is a nephron made of?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is a nephron made of?
body.back: A glomerulus (renal corpuscle) and a renal tubule.
The afferent arteriole is larger than the efferent.

title: What are podocytes and filtration slits?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What are podocytes and filtration slits?
body.back: Inner capsule cells whose foot processes surround the basement membrane; the clefts between them are filtration slits.
Contract to regulate glomerular blood flow; engulf macromolecules trapped during filtration.
Filtration, tubular reabsorption, tubular secretion, water conservation.
2 mL/s, 120 mL/min, about 170 L/day.
About 1 mL/min, 1.5 L/day: 119 of 120 mL/min is reabsorbed.
Binds receptor → cAMP → AQP2 inserted in apical membrane → water reabsorbed by osmosis.

title: Urine with maximal ADH and without ADH?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Urine with maximal ADH and without ADH?
body.back: Max ADH: 0.25 mL/min (375 mL/day). No ADH: 15 mL/min (22.5 L/day).
PCT: ions, water, nutrients, pH; descending limb: water out; ascending limb: Na+ and Cl− out; DCT: ions and pH; collecting duct: water and solutes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fluid advances. Repeating pump and advance multiplies the small difference into a steep gradient.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Saltier interstitium. The medullary interstitium becomes more concentrated deeper in the medulla.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Isosmotic filtrate. Fluid entering the loop is isosmotic (about 300 mOsm) with the interstitial fluid.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Active NaCl pumping. The ascending limb actively transports Na+ (Cl− follows) and is impermeable to water.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Deep medulla. The gradient reaches about 1 200 to 1 400 mOsm at the tip of the loop.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Water leaves the descending limb. Permeable to water, impermeable to ions: water follows by osmosis.
Cortical 85%, short loops, peritubular capillaries. Juxtamedullary 15%, very long loops, vasa recta, concentrate urine.
Transcellular (through cells) and paracellular (between cells, leaky junctions).

title: Primary vs secondary active transport in the PCT?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Primary vs secondary active transport in the PCT?
body.back: Basal Na+–K+ pump uses ATP (primary); apical symports use the Na+ gradient (secondary).
With Na+ by SGLT proteins; normally all of it.
Reabsorbs 65%; microvilli, great length, many mitochondria; 6% of resting ATP; fluid stays isosmotic.

title: Where does the rest of the water go?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Where does the rest of the water go?
body.back: 20% in the descending limb (unregulated); final 15% under hormonal control.
Descending: water yes, solutes no. Ascending: solutes yes (active Na+), water no.

title: Gradient built by the countercurrent multiplier?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Gradient built by the countercurrent multiplier?
body.back: From 300 mOsm in the cortex to about 1 200-1 400 mOsm in the deep medulla.

title: Which structure is at the arrow, and what does it release in stress?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which structure is at the arrow, and what does it release in stress?
body.back: The hypothalamus: its paraventricular nucleus releases CRH.

title: Which gland is at the arrow, and what does it release in stress?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Which gland is at the arrow, and what does it release in stress?
body.back: The pituitary: its anterior lobe releases ACTH, which drives cortisol.

title: Define stressor, stress, hardiness and resilience.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Define stressor, stress, hardiness and resilience.
body.back: Stressor: a condition challenging homeostasis. Stress: the physiological or psychological response to it. Hardiness: coping with acute or chronic stress and staying healthy. Resilience: bouncing back from the initial negative effects.

The paraventricular nucleus releases CRH, the major stimulus for ACTH from the anterior pituitary, which drives cortisol from the adrenal cortex. CRH integrates neural and hormonal signals. Circulating cortisol is the main inhibitor of CRH and ACTH, through gene expression.

title: Name the major brain structures in stress.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the major brain structures in stress.
body.back: Cortex (especially prefrontal); limbic system: amygdala, hippocampus, hypothalamus (receiving PFC and amygdala input); brainstem: medulla (cardiovascular and respiratory responses), locus coeruleus (noradrenaline, arousal) and raphe nuclei (serotonin).

title: Give the major effects of cortisol.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the major effects of cortisol.
body.back: Metabolic: anti-insulin and permissive for glucagon and catecholamines. Vascular: permissive for catecholamines by raising alpha receptors. Immune: anti-inflammatory. Renal: regulates water excretion.

title: How does stress interact with the immune system?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How does stress interact with the immune system?
body.back: Psychoneuroimmunology studies these links. Stress can be pro- or anti-inflammatory via SAM or HPA. Glucocorticoids are first anti-inflammatory, then sensitise the immune response in recovery; CRH regulates immunity; the immune system in turn modulates the HPA axis. Endorphins rise and suppress immunity; growth hormone and prolactin fall.

title: How is the stress response terminated?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How is the stress response terminated?
body.back: Cortisol feedback inhibits CRH and ACTH, and acts on the hippocampus, which turns off the HPA response via the PVN. Lesions along this circuit raise PVN CRH and prolong stress. Factors that damage the hippocampus raise glucocorticoids, which damage it further.

Two-way communication between the brain and gut microbiota via neuroendocrine, neuroimmune and autonomic (vagal) pathways. Stress disturbs the gut ecosystem (for example IBS); gut infection can raise stress responsiveness and brain inflammation. The gut makes 95 percent of the body's serotonin.

title: Give the effects of chronic stress, part 1.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the effects of chronic stress, part 1.
body.back: Chronic stress lasts longer than a month. Nervous and behavioural: dizziness, headache, somatic pain, anxiety, depression, aggression, cognitive impairment, stroke. Cardiovascular: coronary disease, infarction, heart failure, sudden death, tachycardia, dysrhythmias, hypertension. GI: acid and pepsin hypersecretion causing peptic ulcer and GERD. Immune dysfunction.

title: Give the effects of chronic stress, part 2.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the effects of chronic stress, part 2.
body.back: Musculoskeletal: chronic pain, TMJ pain, worse arthritis. Respiratory: asthma, COPD. Reproductive: altered sex hormones and menses, infertility, impotence. Skin: worse lesions, rashes, itching, vasoconstriction and cold skin.

title: What does the biology of resilience show?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What does the biology of resilience show?
body.back: Resilience is a dynamic, lifelong continuum involving stress response systems, neural circuits and immune responses interacting with genes and environment. It involves active protective processes, not just the reversal of harm.
Eustress enhances function. Distress is often persistent and not resolved by coping or adaptation.

title: What is the general adaptation syndrome?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What is the general adaptation syndrome?
body.back: Hans Selye, 1936: stress is the nonspecific response of the body to any demand, running through three stages. The alarm reaction triad: an enlarged adrenal cortex discharging lipid granules; involution of the thymus, spleen and lymph nodes; deep bleeding ulcers in the stomach and duodenum.

Up to 70 percent of primary care visits are estimated to be for stress and lifestyle problems, and the link between mental stress and physical disease is complex and multifactorial. The concept of allostasis and allostatic load describes the cost of repeated adaptation.

Physical: actual disturbances of physiology, such as haemorrhage and infection, processed by the brainstem and hypothalamus, needing an immediate, reflex-like response. Psychological: anticipated threats, such as aversive stimuli, predator cues or unmet drives, engaging the PFC, amygdala, hippocampus, PVN, VTA and nucleus accumbens as well as SN, SAM and HPA.

title: Give the two phases of the stress response.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the two phases of the stress response.
body.back: First: autonomic activation (SN and SAM), rapid, bringing alertness, appraisal and decision making. Second: the hormonal HPA axis, sluggish, but amplified and protracted.

Short (under 2 days to 4 weeks), triggering fight or flight: SN, SAM and HPA are activated and the parasympathetic system diminished. Removing the stressor should restore normality quickly, though sometimes delayed. Examples: danger, trauma, accidents, disasters, crime, witnessing violence.

title: List the four major fight-or-flight responses.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: List the four major fight-or-flight responses.
body.back: 1. Stimulated mental activity. 2. Epinephrine release from the adrenal medulla. 3. Cardiovascular: faster, stronger heart, higher cardiac output, arteriolar constriction in many areas, higher pressure, more blood to muscle and heart, less to gut and kidneys. 4. Metabolic: higher metabolic rate, blood glucose, glycolysis and coagulation rate.

title: Name the adrenal zones and their hormones.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the adrenal zones and their hormones.
body.back: Zona glomerulosa: mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone. Zona fasciculata: glucocorticoids and androgens. Zona reticularis: androgens and glucocorticoids. Medulla: catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine).

title: Why do taste and smell matter in medicine?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Why do taste and smell matter in medicine?
body.back: Many diseases have a characteristic smell or taste, such as sweet diabetic urine or lung cancer; some diseases damage smell, such as allergic rhinitis; electronic noses detect breath VOCs in lung cancer and MRSA. Chemosensory deficits harm nutrition and quality of life.

title: How common are taste and smell disorders?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How common are taste and smell disorders?
body.back: In the US, 7 million adults have taste and 14 million smell disorders; 1 to 2 percent report total loss of smell; 13.9 percent of institutionalised older adults versus 3.2 percent in the community; 400,000 doctor visits a year. Prevalence rises with age.

Addison's disease, periodontal disease, oral infections such as thrush, upper respiratory infections, allergic rhinitis, head trauma, tumours such as vestibular schwannoma, Bell's palsy, vitamin and trace metal deficiencies, wisdom tooth extraction, MS, familial dysautonomia, cancer, radiation, chemotherapy and drugs. Widespread but uncommon.

Olfactory receptor cells are neurons. Odorants bind receptors, afferent fibres carry signals to the olfactory bulb, the first central relay, then to central processing areas. Smells habituate rapidly.

Scrofula: stale beer. Typhoid: baked bread. Yellow fever: a butcher's shop. Diphtheria: sweet. Diabetic ketosis: decomposing apples. Failure to metabolise methionine: boiled cabbage. Hyperaminoaciduria: dried malt or hops.

Qualitative: parosmia (distorted), phantosmia (smell without odour), cacosmia (all odours unpleasant). Quantitative: normosmia, hyposmia (reduced), anosmia (complete or partial loss, acquired or congenital). Agnosia: odours detected but not classified.

Sensitivity and discrimination decline, lowering quality of life, appetite and nutrition. Epithelial neurogenesis falls by about 90 percent in ageing mice; new bulb neurons from the subventricular zone, travelling the rostral migratory stream, also fall. If the basal cell layer survives injury, new cells can still be made.

title: Give the key messages on olfactory disorders.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Give the key messages on olfactory disorders.
body.back: They are common and increase with age. Causes: sinonasal disease, viral infection, head injury, toxins, drugs, autoimmune and neurodegenerative disease. Olfactory loss is an early sign of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. Only nasal causes have causal treatment: surgery or corticosteroids.

title: Name the basic tastes and their meaning.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the basic tastes and their meaning.
