body.back: Salty (NaCl): sodium and osmotic balance. Sweet (sucrose, sweeteners, some proteins): energy. Sour (HCl, tartaric acid): acids. Bitter (quinine): potential toxins. Umami (MSG): savoury, energy-rich food. Fat is a possible sixth taste.
Yes: newborns make different facial expressions to bitter and sweet tastants, so acceptance and rejection need no prior experience.
In papillae on the dorsal and lateral tongue, and on the soft palate, larynx, uvula, pharynx, epiglottis and upper oesophagus.

The chemical must dissolve in saliva and contact the gustatory hairs. Binding depolarises the taste cell, creating a generator potential; voltage-gated Na+, K+ and Ca2+ channels produce action potentials; Ca2+ influx triggers transmitter release. Each taste bud has about 100 cells and responds best to one taste but also to others.

Salty: Na+ enters through a selective channel passing only Na+ and Li+, blocked by amiloride; the generator potential opens basolateral voltage-gated Na+ channels. Sour: H+ enters through PKD2L1, a TRP-type proton channel.
There is evidence for both specific (labelled-line) and distributed coding; some suggest it works like colour vision. There is no agreed explanation yet.
Other receptors, especially smell; the temperature and texture of food; and past experience with food. How the cortex processes taste is still unknown.

Quantitative: ageusia (complete loss), hypogeusia (reduced), hypergeusia (enhanced), each total or partial. Qualitative: parageusia (distorted taste) and phantogeusia (persistent taste with no stimulus).

title: What does the vestibular system do?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: What does the vestibular system do?
body.back: A proprioceptive system for posture, muscle tone, equilibrium and coordination of head and eye movements, and for sensing head position and spatial orientation. Its signals govern reflexes of balance and fixity of gaze.
Kinesthesis: a somatosensory sense of the relative position and motion of body parts. Equilibrium (balance): mediated by the vestibular system. The two work together.

Bipolar neurons in the vestibular ganglion send axons in the vestibular nerve into the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle, ending in the vestibular nuclei. These project to brainstem and upper spinal motor nuclei, the cerebellum and the thalamus, then to cortical areas 2v, 3a, 7 and the parieto-insular vestibular cortex.

title: How does the vestibular system control visual reflexes?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How does the vestibular system control visual reflexes?
body.back: It keeps gaze fixed during head movement through the MLF, linking the vestibular nuclei to the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nuclei and upper spinal motor neurons, and through the vestibulospinal tracts. Abnormal input produces nystagmus.

title: Describe the caloric test and Ménière's disease.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the caloric test and Ménière's disease.
body.back: Caloric test: warm or cold water in the ear canal stimulates the lateral canal crista, producing nystagmus. Ménière's disease: spontaneous high vestibular firing causes dizziness and nausea via the vagal pathway.
An MLF lesion: slowed or absent adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye. Multiple sclerosis can cause it by demyelinating the MLF, with nystagmus and double vision.

An ancient reflex that stabilises the retina by rotating the eyes opposite to head movement. Its long-term adaptation is driven by the cerebellar flocculus, organised in the planes of the canals. The lateral canal drives horizontal eye muscles; the anterior canal drives the ipsilateral superior rectus and contralateral inferior oblique.

In the inner ear, in the petrous temporal bone: a bony and a membranous labyrinth. It senses orientation and motion of the head, not the body, relayed by the vestibular division of CN VIII to the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum.
The otolithic organs, utricle and saccule, detect linear acceleration and gravity, including pitch and roll tilts. The three semicircular canals detect angular acceleration from rotation.

title: How do vestibular hair cells transduce motion?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How do vestibular hair cells transduce motion?
body.back: Stereocilia are embedded in a gel: the otolithic membrane in the maculae, the cupula in the canals. Apices sit in endolymph, basolateral surfaces in perilymph. Bending toward the tallest row opens more transduction channels; away closes them.

The utricular macula lies horizontally and the saccular macula vertically with the head upright, each with a curved striola and differently oriented bundles. Type I and type II hair cells have different innervation. Otoconial weight lets them detect static head orientation and tilt; very loud low-frequency sound can also stimulate them.

title: How does the crista ampullaris respond to rotation?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How does the crista ampullaris respond to rotation?
body.back: At the start of rotation the endolymph lags, tilting the crista opposite to the rotation; on stopping, it tilts in the same direction. At steady velocity the endolymph catches up and the cupula returns to rest. Firing rate rises or falls from its basal level.

title: How do the canals encode direction?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How do the canals encode direction?
body.back: The three canals lie at right angles, covering every direction. Paired canals on the two sides respond oppositely; turning right excites the right lateral canal and inhibits the left. Some vestibular neurons compare both sides, increasing sensitivity.

title: How do the maculae encode tilt?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: How do the maculae encode tilt?
body.back: Upright, afferents on both sides of the striola fire equally. On tilt, displaced otoconia bend the stereocilia: cells on the upward slope fire more, those on the downward slope less. Tilt also triggers ocular counter-roll.

title: Describe the branches of the vestibular nerve.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the branches of the vestibular nerve.
body.back: It divides into superior and inferior divisions joined by an isthmus. Superior (larger): lateral and anterior ampullary nerves, the utricular nerve and part of the saccule. Inferior: the rest of the saccule and the posterior crista via the singular nerve through the foramen singulare.

title: Anatomy link: find the structure for rotation.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Anatomy link: find the structure for rotation.
body.back: The lateral semicircular canal, which senses horizontal head rotation and is the one tested by the caloric test.

title: Anatomy link: find a linear acceleration sensor.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Anatomy link: find a linear acceleration sensor.
body.back: The utricle, whose horizontal macula senses linear acceleration and head tilt.

An object, either a light source or a reflecting surface; light, within the purple to red range; and an eye with photoreceptors, which convert light into action potentials sent to the thalamus, visual cortex and subcortical areas.

Rays travel straight within one medium and bend at a transparent surface. Refraction increases with the difference in refractive index between media and with deviation from a 90-degree angle; a perpendicular ray does not refract. Air has an index of 1.

Filtered plasma from ciliary body epithelium, released into the anterior chamber and reabsorbed through the canal of Schlemm. It nourishes the lens and cornea and sets intraocular pressure, measured by tonometry.
Obstructed drainage, most often at the canal of Schlemm, raises aqueous volume and intraocular pressure. The pressure damages lens proteins and, reaching the retina, can cause loss of vision.

title: Describe the vitreous humour and retinal detachment.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the vitreous humour and retinal detachment.
body.back: A semisolid jelly between lens and retina, present from birth and not renewed. Its fibres shape the eye and hold the retina against the choroid. If its collagen shortens, it pulls the retina off: retinal detachment, an emergency, most often after trauma.

Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonular fibres, so the lens thickens and refractive power rises: near vision, parasympathetic. Ciliary relaxation tenses the fibres and flattens the lens: distant vision. The near response also includes miosis and convergence.

title: Describe presbyopia and the refractive errors.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe presbyopia and the refractive errors.
body.back: Presbyopia: lens proteins denature, the lens loses elasticity, near vision fails; accommodation nears zero after 70. Emmetropia: focus on the retina. Hyperopia: behind it; distance acuity can exceed 1. Myopia: in front. Astigmatism: uneven cornea or lens surface, corrected with cylindrical lenses.
By two-point discrimination, which depends on optical, retinal and stimulus factors. Letter charts are read at 20 feet (6 m); normal is 20/20, or 1. Reading only the largest letter is 20/200.

title: Describe the macula, fovea and optic disc.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the macula, fovea and optic disc.
body.back: The macula and its central fovea give the highest acuity: 2 percent of the retina but a third of ganglion cells, cone-dominated, with fewer overlying layers. The optic disc, where the nerve leaves, has no photoreceptors: the blind spot, filled in by the other eye.

Optic atrophy: ganglion cells degenerate, the disc becomes pale and large, possibly blindness. Papilloedema: raised intracranial pressure pushes the disc forward. Macular degeneration: loss of detailed vision.
Cones: colour vision, high threshold, photopic, dense in the fovea and macula. Rods: black-and-white, scotopic dim-light vision, increasing toward the periphery.

Photoreceptors to bipolar cells to ganglion cells vertically. Horizontal cells carry signals sideways for lateral inhibition at the first synapse; amacrine cells do so at the second; interplexiform cells carry signals backwards to fine-tune lateral inhibition. Ganglion cells fire action potentials; their axons form the optic nerve, crossing at the chiasm. Y ganglion cells transmit fast warning signals.
Refractive power, the inverse of focal length in metres: a 50 cm lens is 2 D. Convex (converging) lenses are positive; concave (diverging) lenses are negative. The eye's lens is biconvex.

title: Name the four refraction points of the eye.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Name the four refraction points of the eye.
body.back: Air to anterior cornea; posterior cornea to aqueous humour; aqueous humour to lens; lens to vitreous humour. Two thirds of the refractive power is in the cornea.

Touch or dust on the richly innervated cornea is sensed by the trigeminal nerve, whose sensory nucleus synapses on the facial motor nucleus. The facial nerve closes the eye and increases lacrimation. A useful CNS test.

title: Describe the sclera, iris and pupil.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the sclera, iris and pupil.
body.back: The sclera is protective fibrous tissue; only the cornea lets light in. The iris gives eye colour, with smooth muscle and pigment layers, and sets pupil diameter. Bright light gives miosis, darkness mydriasis. Sunglasses protect the photoreceptors.
A constricted pupil admits rays through a small area, which focus immediately, giving higher acuity. A dilated pupil scatters rays and blurs detail. The best acuity comes from rays within 5 degrees.

Optic nerve, pretectal area, Edinger-Westphal (parasympathetic) nucleus of CN III, ciliary ganglion, pupil constrictors. In the dark, the sympathetic system dilates the pupil via the cervical ganglion.

Light in one eye constricts that pupil (direct) and the other pupil (consensual or indirect), because the optic pathways decussate. A reflex in only one eye points to CN III. Loss of the reflex after head trauma suggests brainstem damage, near the vital centres.

title: Describe the choroid and ciliary body.
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Describe the choroid and ciliary body.
body.back: The choroid is the vascular layer supplying the eye and helping keep its spherical shape. The ciliary body attaches to the zonular fibres that control lens shape and makes aqueous humour.
The fovea in the macula, where cones dominate and acuity is highest.

title: Anatomy link: which structure sets lens shape?
subject: subj:physio

body.front: Anatomy link: which structure sets lens shape?
body.back: The ciliary body, via its muscle and the zonular fibres; it also makes aqueous humour.
